sections.text:
Methods for observing zooplankton feeding are often limited by their small body size. Fluorescent 
silica nanoparticles (FSNPs) offer a promising alternative because of their bright fluorescence, 
photostability, and observability without the need for sophisticated equipment. To assess their 
potential as fluorescent markers, their physical properties, toxicity, and marking efficiency were 
ascertained using brine shrimp (Artemia franciscana) as a model marine zooplankton. The FSNPs 
were spherical, 64.0 ± 3.9 nm in diameter, and with stable dispersion in seawater. Acute toxicity 
tests showed no significant mortality or immobility in brine shrimp nauplii within 24 h of exposure to 
various FSNP concentrations. Ingested FSNPs exhibited bright luminescence along the gut passage 
under ultraviolet light, with marking efficiency increasing with FSNP concentration. An optimal 
concentration of 16 mg/L provided high fluorescence brightness without affecting locomotion or 
feeding rates. Food facilitated the clearance of FSNPs from the gut, and no observable FSNPs adhered 
to the outer surfaces of the shrimp. However, prolonged or repeated exposure to FSNPs at 16 mg/L 
reduced survival over time. These findings indicate that FSNPs are an effective, nontoxic marker for 
short-term studies of marine zooplankton feeding behavior, providing a valuable tool for ecological 
research.

Keywords  Feeding behavior, Fluorescence, Silica nanoparticle, Tracking, Zooplankton

One major challenge in observing the feeding behavior of zooplankton, especially at the individual level, stems 
from their minuscule body size. A conventional method used so far to study zooplankton feeding is measuring 
the remaining food over a certain period after providing a known amount1–3. The quantity of food consumed 
was  calculated  based  on  the  final  concentration  of  residual  algal  cells  after  feeding  or  the  amount  of  carbon 
or pigments as a proxy for food. The primary results are generally the characteristics of the whole population 
or  sample  group  tested,  and  mathematical  or  statistical  techniques  are  applied  to  infer  those  of  individual 
plankton2,3. Food ingestion can be simply observed under a microscope by mounting plankton on a glass slide 
and their transparent bodies allowing for the observation of food particles traveling through the gut passage4,5. 
However, this method inevitably disturbs or harms the subject which might not reflect its normal behavior. More 
advanced approaches have been developed, in which the test animals must be fixed onto a needle or holder, 
which allows their behavior to be observed either from a video recorded via a macro lens or by electrochemical 
techniques6,7.  It  assesses  not  only  the  feeding  activity  at  the  individual  level  but  also  other  physiological 
characteristics. However, it requires sophisticated apparatus and is not affordable.

Nanotechnology is rapidly becoming a tool in many research areas, including aquatic science. For instance, 
researchers  can  track  the  movement  trajectories  of  small  zooplankton  employing  quantum  dots  (QDs),  a 
fluorescent semiconductor nanocrystal, as well as apply image processing and tracking softwares8,9. The surface 
of  the  QDs  is  modified  for  adherence  to  the  plankton  body,  and  the  tagged  plankton  can  be  located  under 
ultraviolet (UV) light. However, the QDs have not been used to observe feeding activity. Alternatively, in several 
studies, test animals have been allowed to ingest micro or nanoscale fluorescent plastic beads, enabling tracking 
through their digestive tracts10–12. However, their potential toxicity limits their use, as these studies often focus 
on ecotoxicity rather than feeding behavior tracking.

Fluorescent  silica  nanoparticles  (FSNPs)  are  nanosized  silica  particles  that  incorporate  fluorescent  dye 
molecules  within  their  matrix.  They  present  a  promising  alternative  for  observing  the  feeding  behavior  of 
zooplankton owing to their excellent fluorescence brightness and photostability. This characteristic is attributed 
to  the  numerous  dye  molecules  packed  into  a  small  area  within  the  matrix,  which  protects  the  fluorophores 
from oxygen-induced fluorescence bleaching, thus prolonging their usability13,14. In addition, when used in vivo, 
FSNPs prevent direct contact between potentially harmful fluorophores and organisms15. The surface silanol 
groups (≡ Si-OH) also allow for easy modification, enabling cross-linking with biomolecules to act as biosensors, 
achieving specific targeting of certain cells or tissues13,16,17.

One  major  concern  when  applying  marking  materials  in  live  organisms  is  their  potential  toxicity.  Silica 
nanoparticles (SNPs) in their crystalline form are highly toxic and thus are rarely used in biological applications, 
unlike amorphous silica, which is less toxic and more compatible with biological systems18. However, ambiguities 
remain  regarding  the  toxicity  of  amorphous  SNPs,  even  in  the  same  test  organisms19–21.  Among  aquatic 
organisms, the toxicity of SNPs against crustacean zooplankton has mostly been examined in the freshwater flea, 
Daphnia magna, as a representative organism, with varied results22. However, their impacts on other species, 
especially marine zooplankton, have been reported infrequently.

Several factors should be considered when selecting markers for applicability in small animals23. This study 
focused on four key aspects to evaluate the potential of FSNPs as markers for tracking feeding behavior in the 
brine shrimp (Artemia franciscana), which is a nonselective filter feeder, as a representative model for marine 
zooplankton. First, the FSNPs should be able to disperse well in the medium (seawater) to ensure that the target 
organisms can equally access them. Second, they must be nontoxic and do not interfere with normal behavior at 
their working concentration. Third, they must emit a distinct signal that is easily detectable. Finally, they must 
pass through the digestive tract simultaneously with the ingested food and be excreted along with the feces.

Physical characteristics of the FSNPs
FSNPs were spherical with a diameter of 64.0 ± 3.9 nm (n = 90) (Fig. 1a). At an excitation wavelength of 365 nm,

FSNPs in seawater (pH 8.2, conductivity 55.57 mS/cm) was − 59.69 ± 10.67 mV (n = 3), which falls within the 
range for good dispersion stability in the medium24.

compared  to  the  control.  The  immobility  at  48  h  did  not  differ  markedly  among  all  treatments  (χ2  =  13.33, 
df = 11, P = 0.273).

Appropriate FSNP concentration for tracking
Fluorescence due to FSNPs was observed at all tested concentrations. It was observed only in the gut, indicating 
that the FSNPs could not attach to other body parts (Fig. 2 and Supplementary Video 1). The marking efficiency 
was markedly enhanced with an increase in FSNP concentrations until 4 mg/L (Fig. 3a). The presence of food 
did not affect the marking efficiency, but interacted with FSNPs (Table 2).

The  fluorescence  brightness  of  the  marked  individuals  was  influenced  by  FSNP  concentration  and  the 
presence of food (Table 2). The brightness score elevated with an increase in FSNP concentration until 16 mg/L; 
it was greater under the condition of food absence than presence (Fig. 3b). Based on these findings, 16 mg/L 
FSNPs was identified as the optimal concentration (representing the lowest concentration that achieved high 
marking efficiency and fluorescence intensity) and was subsequently used in the following experiments.

The average movement speeds of brine shrimp in the 16 mg/L FSNP suspension (n = 46) and those in the control

96.44 ± 33.06  mm  for  the  FSNP-treated  and  control  groups,  which  were  not  markedly  different  (W = 968.0, 
P = 0.990).

exposure, and continuous exposure groups were 12.8, 11.5, and 8.9 days, respectively. The LT50 for the control 
group (artificial seawater without FSNPs) was not calculated, as 71% of brine shrimp remained alive at the end 
of the experiment. Significant differences in survival curves were observed among the treatment groups (χ² = 
27.4, df = 3, P < 0.001; Fig. 7). Brine shrimp exposed to FSNPs under all treatment conditions exhibited shorter 
lifespan compared to the control group (Supplementary Table 1). When analyzing survival during the first 6 days 
of exposure, significant differences were also detected among the treatment groups (χ² = 13.0, df = 3, P = 0.005). 
However,  only  the  continuous  exposure  group  showed  significantly  lower  survival  compared  to  the  control, 
while the 3-hour and 6-hour intermittent exposure groups did not differ significantly from the control during 
this initial period (Supplementary Table 1).

Throughout the experiment, more than 70% of brine shrimp in the continuous exposure group exhibited 
fluorescence under UV light at each observation point (every 48 h). In contrast, in both the 3-hour and 6-hour 
intermittent exposure groups, fluorescence was detected within 30 min after FSNP administration but was no 
longer detectable after 48 h seawater renewal.

Tests in adults
Fluorescence due to ingested FSNPs can be seen in the abdomen of the adult shrimp (Fig. 8 and Supplementary 
Video 2), while their feces remained as small pellets at the bottom of the container. The average times that the 
shrimp abdomens began to fluoresce after FSNP exposure were 14.4 and 18.8 min for males (n = 25) and females 
(n = 21), respectively. However, they were not significantly different between the sexes (W = 285, P = 0.601). The 
average times that the fluorescent feces appeared due to the excretion of ingested FSNPs were similar between 
males and females (W = 275.5, P = 0.775), which were 38.2 and 39.0 min after providing FSNPs, respectively.

to avoid confounding luminescence signals from the algal chlorophylls (664 and 647 nm for chlorophyll a and 
b, respectively), which have fluorescence peaks close to those of FSNPs (614–617 nm)32. Our results indicated 
that ingested food could reduce the fluorescence signal observed in the gut of brine shrimp. However, at the 
optimal concentration of 16 mg/L, the presence of food no longer had a significant effect on the signal of FSNPs 
(Fig.  3b).  It  should  be  noted  that  a  semi-quantitative  scoring  method  in  our  study  was  performed  to  assess

observer bias and ensure consistency. For more precise and quantitative assessments, imaging systems coupled 
with  fluorescence  intensity  measurements  and  tracking  software,  as  applied  in  previous  studies8,9,  could  be 
utilized in future work. Regarding feeding rate, our findings indicated that FSNPs did not influence the shrimp 
feeding rate. However, it is important to note that yeast is not an ideal diet for brine shrimp because the rigid 
cell walls hinder digestion33. The feeding rates observed in our experiments were low because some yeast cells 
remained undigested and were excreted intact, as indicated by the fluorescence image (Fig. 6b).

Adherence of different types of NPs to the surfaces or appendages of microcrustaceans has been observed, 
including nanoplastics8,9,12. This adherence has been attributed to the surface charges of both the NPs and the 
organisms10. For instance, the use of QDs to track the movements of water fleas required a modification of the 
NP surface to have a positive charge or coated with biotin, facilitating the biotinylation of the water flea cuticle8,9. 
In contrast, in our study, fluorescence microscopy observations revealed that FSNPs were localized exclusively 
in the digestive tracts of brine shrimp, without adherence to other body parts. The zeta potentials of FSNPs in 
seawater indicated a negative charge, mirroring that of the microcrustacean cuticle8. This same charge likely 
prevents the FSNPs from adhering to or penetrating the tissues of brine shrimp due to electrostatic repulsion.

Brine  shrimp  are  nonselective  filter  feeders  that  ingest  particles,  including  food  and  even  sand  grains, 
< 50 μm37. Consequently, FSNPs can be ingested and accumulated in the gut. Although fluorescent micro and 
nanoplastics used have exhibited fluorescence in the gut, which was similar to the objective of our study, they are 
toxic to brine shrimp and have been used to test their negative effects from an environmental perspective rather 
than for feed tracking10,12. Our study demonstrated that a low concentration of FSNPs at 16 mg/L effectively 
allowed  the  observation  of  their  feeding  behavior—using  a  stereomicroscope  for  nauplii  and  with  the  naked 
eye for adults; it showed no adverse impacts on the brine shrimp in our investigations. Thus, we opted for this 
concentration to avoid the excessive use of FSNPs and to reduce the potential negative effects.

By simultaneously providing DAPI-stained yeast and FSNPs as food, we confirmed that both co-travel during 
gut transit and are expelled with normal feces. However, we observed numerous blue dots along the gut wall, 
likely from DAPI molecules binding to the DNA in the nuclei of the epithelial cells. This finding suggests that 
conventional dye staining of food items may not be appropriate for tracking feeding behavior, as the dye can also 
stain the cells, potentially interfering with observations and posing a toxicity risk.

Although  no  acute  toxicity  was  observed,  our  additional  chronic  toxicity  experiments  indicated  that 
continuous and repeated exposure to FSNPs at 16 mg/L induced significant mortality over time. LT50 values of 
FSNPs from our study were similar to those previously reported for A. salina, where LT50 values of 18.8 and 17.9 
days were observed following exposure to SNPs at concentrations of 5 and 10 mg/L, respectively30. Two possible 
mechanisms may account for this delayed toxicity. First, while FSNPs could be excreted from the digestive tract, 
continuous exposure resulted in their persistent presence in the gut, potentially causing blockage that impaired 
food digestion and assimilation, ultimately leading to starvation11. Second, toxic effects of FSNPs as discussed 
earlier  may  emerge  with  repeated  or  prolonged  exposure19,22.  This  could  explain  the  significant  increase  in 
mortality observed in the 3-hour and 6-hour intermittent exposure groups after 6 days, despite the absence of 
detectable accumulation following depuration.

Although this study demonstrated the effects of FSNP exposure on brine shrimp through behavioral and 
survival  assessments,  it  did  not  include  biochemical  or  molecular  biomarkers,  which  could  provide  deeper 
insights into the underlying mechanisms of toxicity. Previous studies have shown that exposure to NPs can alter 
enzymatic  activities  related  to  oxidative  stress  and  detoxification  pathways  in  Artemia,  including  glutathione 
S-transferase (GST), catalase (CAT), and cholinesterase (ChE)38,39. For example, Gambardella et al.39 reported 
that  metal  oxide  NPs  significantly  altered  GST  and  ChE  activities,  even  in  the  absence  of  acute  mortality, 
highlighting their importance in xenobiotic metabolism and neurotoxicity assessment. Similarly, Varó et al.38 
found that amino-modified polystyrene NPs induced oxidative stress and modulated gene expression related 
to  development  (clap),  molting  (cstb),  stress  response  (hsp70),  and  immunity  (proPO  and  lysozyme)  in  A. 
franciscana. Additionally, transcriptomic analyses have shown that exposure to SNPs can affect genes involved 
in stress response and cuticle renewal in aquatic invertebrates40. These findings suggest that prolonged FSNP 
exposure may plausibly affect cellular and molecular pathways in Artemia, even in the absence of apparent acute 
toxicity. Therefore, future studies incorporating gene expression and enzymatic biomarkers would be valuable 
for confirming the mechanistic basis of FSNP-induced stress and toxicity.

Conclusions
This  study  demonstrated  that  FSNPs  present  a  promising  tool  for  observing  the  feeding  behavior  of  marine 
zooplankton. They showed excellent dispersion stability in seawater and exhibited low acute toxicity. Critically, 
they were effectively ingested and expelled by the brine shrimp, allowing for a clear observation of the feeding 
processes without adhering to the shrimp’s outer surfaces or causing significant adverse effects. Our findings 
indicate that FSNPs can be utilized to track the passage of ingested food through the gut, providing valuable 
insights into the feeding behavior of zooplankton. FSNPs at 16 mg/L were sufficient to mark the shrimp without 
affecting  their  locomotion  during  short  time  exposure.  However,  prolonged  or  repeated  exposure  negatively 
affected survival, indicating potential long-term risks. The presence of food facilitated the clearance of FSNPs 
from their digestive tract. Their ease of observation under UV light makes them particularly useful for such

Materials and methods
Nanoparticle characterization
FSNPs were synthesized according to the method outlined by Songvorawit, et al.15 using the water-in-oil reverse 
microemulsion  technique,  and  Rubpy  dye  (tris  [2,2′-bipyridyl]ruthenium[II]  chloride)  as  a  fluorophore.  The 
NPs  were  examined  under  a  JEM-1400  transmission  electron  microscope  (TEM;  JEOL,  Tokyo,  Japan),  and 
their  size  was  measured  from  the  TEM  images  employing  the  ImageJ  software  version  1.53o  (NIH,  USA; 
https://imagej.nih.gov/ij). Since this study used FSNPs suspended in saline water, their dispersion stability was 
examined in artificial seawater (ASTM D1141-98, pH 8.2) utilizing a Nano ZSP zeta-sizer (Malvern Panalytical, 
Great Malvern, England). Emission spectra were examined employing a Duetta™ fluorometer (Horiba Scientific, 
Kyoto, Japan) at excitation bands of 365 and 460 nm, which corresponded to the UV light wavelength used to 
track animal behavior in this study and the maximal excitation wavelength of Rubpy dye, respectively14. The 
maximal emission wavelength of the FSNPs was calculated using a moving average based on five data points.

Test animals and handling
Commercial  brine  shrimp  (Artemia  franciscana)  cysts  (American  Eagle,  USA)  imported  from  the  Great  Salt 
Lake, USA were purchased from a local supplier in Bangkok, Thailand. They were hatched in artificial seawater 
at 25–26 °C under continuous aeration and illumination. For rearing adult shrimp, nauplii (shrimp larvae) were 
transferred into an 8 L tank and raised in filtered natural seawater (3% salinity) at 25–26 °C under continuous 
aeration and a light intensity of 1,600 lx (fluorescent lamp) under a 12/12 h illumination cycle. Artificial food 
(composition unknown, branded as N.P. Guppy, Thailand) purchased from a local seller in Bangkok, Thailand, 
was provided every other day, and the adults were obtained 3 weeks after hatching.

Euthanasia was performed utilizing the two-step method (immersion in 5% ethanol for 5 min and then 10% 
formalin) per the AVMA guidelines41. The experimental protocol was approved by the Animal Care and Use 
Committee of the Faculty of Science, Chulalongkorn University (Protocol Review No. 2423018).

Acute toxicity test
Nauplii,  18–24  h  post-hatching,  were  transferred  into  24-well  plates  containing  1–1,024  mg/L  of  FSNP 
suspension  in  artificial  seawater  (2  mL  of  suspension  and  10–20  nauplii  per  well)  and  cultured  at  25–26  °C 
under a light intensity of 1,600 lx (fluorescent lamp) with a 12/12 h light/dark cycle. Brine shrimp grown in 
artificial seawater without FSNPs were used as a control. Mortality and immobility were checked at 24 and 48 h 
after exposure. A nauplius was considered dead if its appendages stopped moving within 10 s. Immobility was 
identified when a nauplius remained with moving appendages in situ for 10 s and was calculated by dividing 
the number of immobile (but still alive) individuals by the total number of living individuals. A mortality rate 
in the 24-h period of less than 10% was considered valid for the control group. Each treatment was conducted 
in eight replications.

Test for the appropriate FSNP concentration for tracking

were used. They were incubated in 2 mL of FSNP suspension in 24-well plates for 1 h at 25–26 °C in the dark under 
two conditions: food presence (1 × 106 cells/mL of baker’s yeast) or food absence. They were then euthanized. 
The fluorescence due to FSNP intake, which was visible through the body wall, was inspected under a stereo 
microscope coupled with a UV lamp set to 365 nm. To minimize observer bias, the same examiner conducted 
all observations throughout the experiment. The fluorescence brightness was scored on a scale ranging from 0 
to 2: 0 = no, 1 = slight, and 2 = bright fluorescence (Fig. 2). The marking efficiency was calculated following the

Chronic toxicity test
Based  on  the  results  of  the  appropriate  FSNP  concentration  experiment,  a  concentration  of  16  mg/L  FSNPs 
was used for the chronic toxicity test. Brine shrimp nauplii (18–24 h post-hatching) were transferred to 250 mL 
Erlenmeyer flasks containing 150 mL of artificial seawater under continuous aeration, with 10 nauplii per flask. 
They were fed with artificial food, and both seawater and food were renewed every 48 h. Three treatment groups 
were performed: (1) continuous exposure to FSNPs, (2) 3-hour exposure to FSNPs every 48 h, and (3) 6-hour 
exposure to FSNPs every 48 h. In treatments (2) and (3), nauplii were exposed to FSNPs prior to the renewal of 
seawater and food. The experiment was conducted over a period of 14 days. A control group was maintained 
in artificial seawater without FSNPs. Rearing conditions and mortality assessment criteria were consistent with 
those used in the acute toxicity test. Each treatment was conducted in nine replications.

Test with adult brine shrimp
Adult brine shrimp, 25 males and 24 females, were used to evaluate whether FSNPs could be applied to developed 
stages. The sexes were determined by the presence of a clasping organ (male) and brood sac (female). The shrimp 
were randomly selected from an aquarium and transferred into 24-well plates filled with 2 mL of baker’s yeast 
suspension  (1 × 106  cells/mL),  one  individual  per  well.  They  were  dark-acclimatized  for  30  min.  The  FSNP 
suspension was then added to each well to reach a final NP concentration of 16 mg/L. Observations were made 
every 5 min under UV light to detect the appearance of abdominal fluorescence, followed by further monitoring 
until luminescent feces were detected, indicating complete gut passage of the ingested FSNPs.

Statistical analyses
Because our data did not meet the assumption for parametric statistics, nonparametric statistical analyses were 
used in all tests. The effects of FSNP concentration on mortality and immobility were ascertained by applying 
the  Kruskal–Wallis  test;  Dunn’s  test  was  used  for  pairwise  comparison.  The  effects  of  FSNP  concentration, 
the presence or absence of food, and their interaction with the marking efficiency or fluorescence brightness 
of  the  marked  individuals  were  analyzed  employing  the  aligned  rank  test.  Feeding  rates  in  the  presence  and 
absence of FSNPs were corrected for the rate of yeast autolysis in the control group and then compared by the 
Wilcoxon rank-sum test. The effects of depuration time, the presence or absence of food, and their interactions 
were analyzed using the aligned rank and Dunn’s tests. Locomotion data for shrimp treated with FSNPs were 
compared  with  the  control  utilizing  the  Wilcoxon  rank-sum  test. The  number  of  times  that  the  abdomen  of 
adult brine shrimp exhibited luminescence and the number of  times that  the fluorescent feces appeared due 
to the excretion of FSNPs were compared between sexes using the Wilcoxon rank-sum test. LT50 was analyzed 
using probit analysis in SPSS version 28.044. All other statistical analyses were performed using the base, ARTool, 
combinate, dplyr, survival, survminer, and tidyverse packages in R, version 4.3.045.
